extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students and scholars of drama and creative writers interested in tragic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic poetry/drama focusing on plot construction, character, and the elements that produce pity and fear according to classical poetics (Aristotle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs History (universality vs particularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry tends to express the universal, history the particular; the poet relates what may happen, the historian what has happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for universals that show how a person of given character will act or speak under circumstances (the poet's work is to present types of possible action rather than merely recounting particular factual events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Possibility of Events
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in poetry should be possible or probable according to the law of probability or necessity; credibility depends on seeming possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer actions which appear likely or necessary consequences of preceding events; avoid incidents that seem impossible or random without justification (what has happened is manifestly possible; invented events should retain internal probability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Names and Fictitious vs Real Subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy commonly invents names and incidents; tragedians often keep to real names because what is possible is credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet may invent names or alter legends, but need not slavishly adhere to received legends; inventiveness is allowed provided the incidents retain probability and produce pleasure for a wide audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (maker of plots)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet or 'maker' should be the maker of plots rather than of verses, since he imitates actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize construction of action and causal sequence over merely decorative language or versification; the plot is the essential determining feature of poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Epeisodic Plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'epeisodic' plot is one in which episodes succeed without probable or necessary sequence and is the worst kind of plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure continuity and causal/narrative necessity between episodes; avoid strings of loosely connected scenes produced simply to extend performance or please actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of Complete Action and the Terrible & Pitiful
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates complete action and events terrible and pitiful; its distinctive mark is to excite pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select actions that can arouse pity and fear and compose them into a complete, unified sequence with a clear beginning, middle, and end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise Combined with Causal Connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects are best produced when events come by surprise and at the same time follow from one another; the tragic wonder is greater when events seem designed rather than accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct surprises that nonetheless are the necessary or probable consequences of earlier actions; avoid mere accidents or monstrously spectacular devices unconnected to plot logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple versus Complicated Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are Simple (turning point without Reversal or Recognition) or Complicated (with Reversal of Fortune, or Recognition, or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using complication, have reversals and recognitions arise from the internal structure of the plot so that later events are necessary or probable results of earlier ones; prefer simple unified design for greatest effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of Fortune (Peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Reversal of Fortune is a change by which a train of action produces the opposite of the effect intended, according to probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reversals so they follow naturally and inevitably (or probably) from preceding actions; examples include the messenger in Oedipus aiming to comfort but causing ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate; best when coincident with a reversal of fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognition especially when it arises organically from the plot and connects to reversal to intensify pity and fear; recognitions may be of persons, facts, or signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Incident
rubrics_metrics.description: A Tragic Incident is a destructive or painful action (death on stage, bodily torments, wounds, etc.) forming part of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include incidents of suffering where appropriate, but ensure they are motivated by plot and character, not gratuitous spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative Parts of Tragedy (structural elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into Prologos, Episode, Exodos, and Choral elements (Parodos and Stasimon); also songs of actors and the Commos (joint lament).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the work into these parts and use each consistently with its definition (Prologos precedes Parodos, Episodes between choral songs, Exodos follows with no choral song after it, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for the Simple (single) Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect tragedy should be arranged on the simple, not the complicated, plan and should imitate actions which excite pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor a single unified plot over double-threaded or episodic structures (the latter often cater to spectators' weakness and belong more to comedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Moral Standing of Protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should not be the spectacle of a perfectly good man brought to adversity, nor the utter villain's downfall; best is a man neither eminently good nor villainous whose misfortune arises from error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose protagonists of high repute or standing who fall through hamartia (error/frailty) rather than vice, to arouse pity and fear (examples: Oedipus, Thyestes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction of Change of Fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should be from good to bad (prosperity to adversity), not from bad to good or vice versa for villains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure reversal so the protagonist falls from prosperity to misfortune through error, not through sheer vice or reward of villainy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner Structure over Spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity should ideally be aroused by the inner structure of the piece so that even when merely told the story it produces horror and pity; relying on spectacle is a less artistic method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize plot and character construction to evoke emotions; avoid dependence on sensational scenic effects or monstrous spectacle that are extraneous to the plot's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of Relationships for Tragic Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of producing pity or fear must occur between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent, but strongest when between those near or dear (kin or close relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek incidents involving kinship/friendship (brother vs brother, son vs father, mother vs son) to maximize tragic poignancy; enemy-against-enemy produces little pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for and Skillful Use of Traditional Material
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should not destroy the framework of received legends (e.g., Clytemnestra slain by Orestes) but should invent and adapt traditional material skilfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain recognisable core facts of myths while exercising creative invention to produce effective tragic situations; 'use the received legends well'—adaptation must preserve plausibility and tragic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred Modes for the Horrible Deed (timing & recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible modes: (a) deed done with full knowledge (older poets), (b) deed done in ignorance with recognition afterwards (effective), (c) about to do deed and discover before act (best when recognition spares act) — but being about to act knowing consequences and then refraining is shocking not tragic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most effective tragic arrangements are those where the deed is committed in ignorance and recognized afterwards, or where recognition occurs just before action and prevents it (timing affects tragic quality); avoid scenarios where no consequence follows (shocking but not tragic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot Causality: No Irrationality Within Action
rubrics_metrics.description: The unfolding of the plot must come about from the plot itself (necessity or probability); machinery (deus ex machina) is only for events external to the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid internal irrational devices; if impossibilities appear, place them outside the action (previous events or things to be announced) rather than using miraculous contrivances within the plot's interior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Machinery (external devices) Limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Machinery should be employed only for events external to the drama—previous to it or subsequent to it and needing announcement; not for internal resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve central plot developments by gods or improbable machinery; let the plot's internal logic resolve itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: Four Aims
rubrics_metrics.description: In characterization aim for (1) goodness, (2) propriety (fit between character and role), (3) likeness to life (truth/realism), (4) consistency (even consistent inconsistency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters' speech and actions demonstrate moral purpose; characters should be appropriate to sex/status, true to life, and behave consistently within their type (avoid incongruous traits or inconsistent development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Actions Follow Necessity or Probability
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of given character should speak or act in a given way by the rule either of necessity or of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters' choices and utterances logically follow from their established dispositions; avoid behaviour that contradicts their shown nature unless duly motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Incongruity and Inconsistency in Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must not display inappropriate, incongruous or needlessly bad traits that undermine pity/fear (examples: Menelaus in Orestes, inconsistent Iphigenia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against lapses where a character behaves in ways that clash with earlier presentation; preserve the unity of character or make any departures clearly motivated by plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory and Non-Essential Concomitants
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the senses (spectacle, stagecraft) are concomitants of poetry and not among the essentials, though they offer scope for error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenic and sensory elements prudently to support the plot's emotional aims, but do not substitute spectacle for structural or character-based tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by Signs (least artistic form)
rubrics_metrics.description: One kind of recognition is by signs (congenital items like a spear), often the least artistic form used where wit is poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that arise from plot and character rather than contrived tokens; use signs only when they serve the internal probability of the story.
